Ag+ with anion forms precipitate: possibilities: Cl- (AgCl white), Br- (AgBr pale yellow), I- (AgI yellow), S2- (Ag2S black), CO3^2- (Ag2CO3 white), etc. White precipitate suggests AgCl, Ag2CO3, Ag2SO4 (white), Ag2S is black, AgI yellow. So likely Cl- or CO3^2- or SO4^2-.

We added NH3 (5M) to the mixture; precipitate did not dissolve. AgCl is insoluble in NH3 (only slight solubility? Actually AgCl dissolves in concentrated NH3 to form [Ag(NH3)2]+, but moderate? Usually AgCl dissolves in NH3, forming complex, but may need excess. However typical qualitative test: AgCl does not dissolve in dilute NH3, but does in concentrated NH3. Here we added 1 mL of 5M NH3 to mixture (total volume ~3 mL). That's fairly concentrated. If precipitate remained, suggests it's not AgCl (since would dissolve). But maybe not enough? Could be Ag2SO4 also insoluble in NH3. Ag2CO3 also dissolves in NH3? I think Ag2CO3 dissolves in NH3 as well. Actually Ag2CO3 is soluble in NH3 forming complex. So persistent white precipitate suggests maybe Ag2SO4? But Ag2SO4 is slightly soluble, but not precipitate normally? Reaction of AgNO3 with sulfate gives white precipitate of Ag2SO4? Actually Ag2SO4 is sparingly soluble, may precipitate. It is not soluble in NH3. So anion could be SO4^2-.

But we also have Na+; Na2SO4 is soluble, but the unknown salt could be Na2SO4. That would give Na+ (yellow flame) and sulfate. Adding AgNO3 to Na2SO4 yields Ag2SO4 precipitate (white). Adding NH3 does not dissolve. So consistent.

We should also test with Ba(NO3)2 to see if sulfate gives white precipitate of BaSO4 (insoluble). Let's do that.
